extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of early-18th-century periodical literature; students of Steele/The Tatler; general literary readers
extracted.subtask_description: An annotated/edited reprint of Steele's Tatler essays (early 18th century) containing literary criticism, social commentary, and explanatory footnotes for readers and scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic character representation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the character which gives name to the play, there is excellently represented the reluctance of a battered debauchee to come into the trammels of order and decency: he neither languishes nor burns, but frets for love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is given where characters convincingly embody motivations and moral dispositions; effective dramatic characters show believable internal conflict (e.g., a reformed rake who 'frets for love' rather than theatrically languishing). Use concrete, nuanced behaviours rather than melodramatic signs of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness of dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: The drama introduced by the dialogue of the first scene with uncommon, yet natural conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue should feel natural and conversational while still serving dramatic purpose; a strong opening scene uses realistic speech to introduce plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirited rendering of supporting characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The gentlemen of more regular behaviour are drawn with much spirit and wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary figures should be sketched vividly and wittily so they contribute energy and contrast to main characters rather than being flat or perfunctory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aptness of characterization to social types
rubrics_metrics.description: The part of Fondlewife is a lively image of the unseasonable fondness of age and impotence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should appropriately reflect recognizable social types or follies in a way that illuminates theme (e.g., age, impotence, vanity) rather than caricature without insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'easy writing' and trivial versifying
rubrics_metrics.description: These jaunty scribblers ... are so justly laughed at for their sonnets on Phillis and Chloris, and fantastical descriptions in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject facile, conventional conceits and overly sweet sonnets/pastoral clichés that require little craft. Aim for workmanship that resists being dismissible as 'easy writing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer realism/verisimilitude over artificial invention
rubrics_metrics.description: He never forms fields, or nymphs, or groves, where they are not, but makes the incidents just as they really appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict scenes and incidents as they actually occur in the author's context (e.g., an urban 'Description of the Morning') instead of inventing pastoral or romantic scenery where it does not belong; specificity and truth-to-life are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality; discourage imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: I bar all descriptions of the evenings; ... I forewarn also all persons from encouraging any draughts after my cousin ... I will not admit of counterfeits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid imitating fashionable or overused descriptions and characters; editors/critic-publications should call out and discourage 'counterfeits' and imitators to maintain originality in taste and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodical's critical function: expose pretence and distinguish merit
rubrics_metrics.description: To examine who and who are together, to tell any mistaken man he is not what he believes he is, to distinguish merit, and expose false pretences to it, is a liberty our family has by law in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial mission includes social criticism: identifying true merit, revealing pretence, and correcting public misconception. This grounds the essay-paper's remit to judge and to name social behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect moral reform through example and subtle management
rubrics_metrics.description: The good lady ... intended to watch her, and take some opportunity of engaging her insensibly in her own interests, without the anguish of an admonition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking to reform manners or behaviour (here, of a young woman), prefer indirect methods—engaging interests, modelling desirable conduct—over harsh admonition; pedagogical subtlety is praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should be just and finely wrought
rubrics_metrics.description: Where all our little weaknesses are laid open in a manner more just, and with, truer raillery than ever man yet hit upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire is commended when it exposes weaknesses with fairness and deft humour rather than crude invective; 'truer raillery' combines precision, justice, and witty tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject unrealistic prescriptive schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing he makes this gentleman propose, is, that she shall be no woman; ... I have not patience with these unreasonable expectations, therefore turn back to the treatise itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive proposals (e.g., schemes for governing a wife) should be sensible and respectful of human nature; extravagant or impossible prescriptions are to be criticized and set aside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of beauty/love as a credible motivating device
rubrics_metrics.description: Every temper, except downright insipid, is to be animated and softened by the influence of beauty: but of this untractable sort is a lifeless handsome fellow ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In character construction, beauty or romantic attachment can plausibly motivate transformation or soften temperament; use it as a credible human influence rather than a mere plot contrivance.
